subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module with the SDK for a cat-sized dragon, roughly 0.45m long, sitting beside a cracked broken egg, grounded at y=0, with a few small translucent spheres suggesting wisps of smoke.

For materials I'm using countershade and spots paint for a speckled egg texture, and simple amber-and-black sphere eyes instead of complex decals. I'm working out the skeleton now, starting from the hips joint positioned low near the ground and building a spine chain curving upward into the chest to give the dragon an upright, sitting posture.

Still building the joint chain...

I'm working out the jaw joint position and the head's orientation, aiming it slightly forward and upward so the local axes (forward, up, right) align sensibly with the model's world coordinates.

For the head shapes themselves, I'm sketching the cranium as a scaled sphere primitive, slightly flattened, as a stylized placeholder rather than trying to model exact anatomy.

Now I'm working out the snout and jaw: an upper jaw box attached forward from the head, and a separate jaw joint positioned near the back of the snout so it can hinge open, using the head's local coordinate helper to place and aim it.

Still working through jaw geometry...

I'm untangling the left/right sign conventions for head.local coordinates versus model space, deciding it doesn't matter much for symmetric features but picking one side arbitrarily for asymmetric details like nostril smoke.

I'll simplify by using named-word offsets on head.local instead of raw coordinates—keys like right, forward, up, left, down, back—mirroring across sides with a sign multiplier on the left value, then move on to positioning the eyes.

Placing the amber eye sphere offset to the side, up, and slightly forward of the head, then adding a small dark pupil sphere nudged further forward so it protrudes slightly from the eye's surface, keeping proportions so the eye sits near the edge of the cranium.

Now I'm working out the wings, attaching them at the shoulder joint on the spine so they're oversized and membrane-like, folded slightly rather than fully spread since the creature can't fly yet — building out the shoulder-to-elbow-to-wrist chain for the wing arm's pose.

Still defining finger capsules...

Still defining membrane edges...

Settling on a simpler approach: one membrane fanning from the wrist to fingers one and three, plus a separate membrane connecting the elbow and body to fill out the wing shape near the torso.

For coloring, I'm layering a mottled teal pattern for the back that fades into a buttery countershaded belly, possibly nesting mottle inside the countershade paint. For the spine, I'm planning a row of orange spines running down the back using the along function.

Now I'm thinking spines need to poke out from the body's surface rather than sit at the chain's centerline, since starting them there would bury them inside the body radius — so I need to find the right surface offset so they emerge properly from the dorsal line.

Defining the radius function...

I need to double check the hip placement so the sitting dragon's pelvis actually rests near the floor rather than floating—adjusting hips to around y=0.11 so the bottom of that hip sphere meets the ground properly.

Now I'm building the legs for the sitting pose: thighs as scaled spheres near the hips, shins as capsules angling forward to flat feet resting on the floor at the front.

I'm also reconsidering the leg structure as a proper joint chain for rigging — naming hip, knee, and ankle joints so the creature lab can treat each leg as a bendable kinematic chain rather than static primitives.

I'll simplify the foot to a scaled sphere positioned near the ankle bone, flattened and elongated to suggest a foot shape. Then I'll move on to designing the arms as a small chain with claws running from the shoulder joint outward.

For the limbs, I'm distinguishing separate shoulder-rooted chains for wings versus arms so names don't collide, giving each its own joint naming scheme and role tag. Then I'm adding tiny spike-like claws at the wrist tips using small cone shapes to suggest fingers.

Now I'm working out the spine-to-neck-to-head hierarchy, mapping out joint positions along the spine chain and deciding where the neck chain branches off, then placing the head joint with an aim direction so it tilts upward and outward naturally.

For the wings, I'm positioning the shoulder joint near the upper spine, then working out the elbow and wrist points spread outward and drooping slightly, and starting to lay out the finger bones radiating from the wrist to form the spread of the wing membrane.

Still defining wing points...

Setting the wrist as the wing chain's tip joint, then planning the tail geometry as a curved chain from hips to a spade-like tip, with three segments named for each tail joint.

Defining a diamond-shaped spade outline extruded along the X-Y plane with smoothing, positioned at the tail's tip to form the arrowhead end...

Adjusting the tail tip to sit lower at y 0.07 with the spade top around 0.2 for a cuter look. For the head, I'll keep stubby horns and subtle brow/cheek details. For nostril smoke, I'm planning small spheres of increasing radius drifting upward along a bezier curve path from the nostril position.

Now working out the snout geometry: positioning the upper jaw box relative to the head bone, and figuring out how parts without explicit orientation default to aligning with the model's world axes versus the bone's local frame.

Setting up the lower jaw next, placing the joint position and aim point on the head, then adding a lower jaw box part.

Still placing teeth and spikes... For eyes I'll use an amber sphere with a dark pupil, and add small brow horns above using the spike function with a brownish horn color.

Now I'm positioning the brow horns to lean outward and back based on which side of the head they're on, then adding seven orange spikes along the spine. For the companion egg, I'm planning a lathed profile for the egg shape with a speckled paint pattern in cream and brown tones.

I'm adding speckled texture to the egg using spot-paint over the lathe shape, then moving on to design the broken shell fragment — shaping its outer wall as a bowl with a jagged sawtooth rim going from the base up and around to simulate a cracked edge.

Still shaping the jagged rim...

Checking that crossing one more time confirms no overlap between the inner and outer walls. Now I'm thinking about the shell's coloring — cream with speckles to match the egg — and positioning the egg shell next to the dragon's body, roughly offset to the side so it doesn't collide with the dragon's hips.

Since the request only calls for the broken shell beside the dragon, I'll skip the whole egg and just lathe the broken shell shape at a position off to one side. I'll keep smoothing at 0 and add more points along the curve to preserve the sharp broken rim without risking edge-crossing errors from excessive smoothing.

For extra realism, I'll scatter a couple tiny shell fragments on the ground near the shell using small scaled dodecahedron shapes positioned and oriented to sit flush against the floor.

Checking that nothing clips below y=0 — feet, shell, and shards all land within the allowed small sink tolerance. Now I'm settling on the color palette: teal and deep teal for the body, buttery cream and orange/amber accents, amber eyes with dark pupils, and bone-white for the shell.

Working through the paint logic: countershading the mottled teal/deep-teal body with a butter underside, applying it along the spine sweep so thickness tapers with a sine curve, and confirming the chain-based sweep handles the roll correctly without needing a separate bone reference.

Now I'm building the leg chains symmetrically for left and right sides, defining hip-knee-ankle points with tapering radii, and adding thigh sphere bulges at the hip joints for shape.

For the feet, I'm attaching flattened spheres to the ankle tip of each leg, then spacing out small toe spheres along the front of the foot.

Now I'm building the arm chains, deciding on shoulder-elbow-wrist joint positions so the arms raise forward with hands reaching out in front rather than tucked against the chest.

Adding small claw spikes near the hand base for a cute touch, then moving on to building the wings.

I'm setting up a wing chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the spine, tagging it with a wing role, then sweeping the upper arm bone with a tapering thickness profile.

Now I'm positioning the actual joint coordinates for shoulder, elbow, and wrist, then placing finger tips extending from the wrist to create the fanned-out wing shape.

Still figuring out membrane attachment points...

The skin should be translucent amber using that hex color. For the finger capsules, I'm connecting wrist points to fingertips with tapered radii, colored teal and bound to the wing tip bone. Then I need to add spines along the torso sweep using the along function with spike callbacks between 10% and 90% of the spine length.

Setting up the dorsal spikes with small soft-orange cones, then building the neck as a tapering sweep from the upper spine point outward and upward, and defining the head joint attached to the neck's second segment with an aim direction forward.

Now I'm positioning the snout as a box jutting forward from the skull, checking that it overlaps properly with the cranium's front edge rather than floating separately.

For the jaw, I'm defining a hinge joint near the head's base with the lower jaw box angled slightly downward and matching the body color, treating it as its own bone attached to the jaw joint.

For the teeth, I'm working out symmetric left/right positions along the upper row using small offset increments so each tooth sits evenly spaced relative to the jaw's forward and vertical placement.

Placing symmetric eyes and pupils...

Actually forward-facing would read better visually, so I'll reposition the eyes slightly more toward the front of the skull, with the pupil placed along the outward vector from the eye sphere's center so it properly protrudes toward the viewer.

Still defining horn placement and geometry... checking I'll skip cheek frills and ear fins for simplicity but keep a crest of spines, then move to positioning the nostrils and sketching the smoke trail as a bezier path curving outward from each nostril.

Adding more smoke puff positions and the shell paint, using a speckled pattern over the cream base color via the spots function.

Still working out the lathe outline...

I'm checking whether these rim zigzag segments accidentally intersect the inner wall line, working through the coordinates parametrically to verify the two segments don't cross each other.

Given the risk of the zigzag crossing, I'll simplify by reducing the number of points in the sawtooth pattern to avoid the collision entirely.

Checking that the shell's outer and inner boundary points stay properly separated near the base so the polygon doesn't self-intersect, then confirming the closing edge degenerates harmlessly. The shape works as a standalone shell without needing the full egg, so I'll position it in the scene at roughly [-0.34, 0, 0.1].

I'm setting up spot and mottle paint patterns for the shell and body—speckles over the egg surface, teal-to-butter countershading for the belly fade, and orange spikes for the spines. For the tail, I'm defining a chain of points running from the hips through tail segments to a tip, using a catmull spline so the path curves smoothly, then sweeping a tapering radius along it to give a chubby base that narrows toward the tip.

Now I'm figuring out how the tail's spade shape should be oriented—deciding the extrusion plane and axis directions so the spade plate faces sideways rather than edge-on, picking the right x/y basis vectors so it reads properly from a side view, then starting to lay out the actual outline points for the spade shape in the z-y plane.

Since no bone array is given, it should default to the nearest joint, likely the tail tip — I'll specify bone: tail.tip explicitly to be safe. I should double check all referenced joints actually exist: hips, spine, neck, head, jaw.

Since chain.tip might be null, I'll fall back to the last joint in tail.joints instead of risking a type error. I'll also check spine indices and joint roles like "head" to make sure they align correctly.

I need to be careful about unused imports since the project likely enforces noUnusedLocals, so I'll only import the functions I actually use from the builder library — things like createBuilder, bezier, catmull, polyline, spots, countershade, and mottle, avoiding rng unless randomness is needed.

Defining color palette constants...

Still building the skeleton hierarchy...

Checking that the spine chain's starting point duplicates the hips position matches the pattern from the docs, so that's fine. Now I'm setting up the neck chain next, continuing from the spine's endpoint.

Continuing the joint hierarchy with the head attached to the neck's second joint, and the jaw attached to the head using local offsets for position and aim — confirming the local() method correctly returns a Vector3 that's accepted as point input.

For the legs, I'm setting up a mirrored loop over left/right sides where positive X is left, building a chain from hip to knee to ankle using a polyline of three points, and checking that the names array properly maps to the hip, knee, and tip ankle joints.

Now I'm defining the arm chain similarly, attaching it as a child of the spine's third joint and naming shoulder, elbow, and wrist. Then I set up the wing chain off the same spine joint with wing-specific shoulder, elbow, and wrist names, and begin constructing the tail using a catmull spline for smoother curvature.

I'm checking that each chain's joint count matches its name array — the tail gets four points for three segments plus a tip, which checks out. Then I'm verifying spine and neck chains follow the same point-to-name convention before moving to the body geometry: I'm sweeping the spine with a radius function that bulges slightly using a sine curve to suggest a chubby belly, adjusting the base and amplitude values for a rounder look, and starting the neck sweep next.

Setting up neck, tail, and leg sweeps with tapering radius functions, then adding hip and foot spheres with scaled proportions and positioning toes at the front of each foot so they sit just inside the foot's forward edge.

Now I'm adding arms with a tapering sweep, a hand sphere scaled for shape, and claw spikes positioned along the front of the hand using point and direction vectors.

Moving to the wings now, I'm setting up a tapering sweep for the wing bone and starting to work out the finger joints and wrist point along the wing.

Writing finger capsule code...

I should connect membrane edges from the wrist root out to each fingertip rather than between the two fingertips, since each edge needs to form a proper polyline from base to tip for resampling.

That fan shape works for the bat wing, so I'll set the membrane color to translucent amber and add a row of spikes along the torso's back using an orange spike generator spaced between about 12% and 92% of its length.

Now I'm adding stubby horns near the head using a local offset per side with a mirrored direction vector, and positioning amber eye spheres at a symmetric offset on the head.

Checking that the pupils sit slightly proud of the eye surface so they're visible rather than sunk in, then placing the snout as a box attached to the head bone with a forward offset for the muzzle shape.

Now I'm positioning the lower jaw as a box attached to the jaw bone, offset forward and down so its top edge lines up with the jaw joint, and giving it a butter color.

Then I'm placing upper teeth as small spikes spaced along the snout's bottom edge, keeping them within the snout box's width, and doing the same for lower teeth attached to the jaw bone, both colored bone-white.

Next I'm working on a smoke effect emerging from the head, computing a starting point and building a bezier curve that curls upward and outward from it.

Building puff spheres along the curve...

Smoke puffs look fine starting small. Now I'm adding an egg shell shape using a lathe revolution with a defined outline, positioned and colored to match the paint, with smoothing off and 14 segments for a faceted look.

Checking the shard pieces around the shell using scaled dodecahedron geometry placed near the egg's edges so they read as broken fragments rather than overlapping the body awkwardly, and confirming the egg paint uses a speckled texture pattern that's compatible with the lathe's color option.

I'm doing a scale sanity check: dragon height roughly 0.6 with wingspan reaching wide extents, comparable to a sitting cat, with the egg shell proportioned sensibly against the head size. I'm confirming the paint functions (spots, mottle, countershade) and curve utilities (bezier, catmull, polyline) are all being used correctly, and double-checking that the `along` helper's options and callback return types won't cause type errors.

Now I'm working out the tail spade geometry, extruding an outline shape at the tail tip with proper bone attachment and amber coloring, making sure the outline points are typed correctly for the extrude call and that the spade's base width matches the tail's tube diameter so it sits naturally at the end.

With the spade oriented properly, I'm moving on to writing out the full final code, checking joint roles for spine, neck, and tail chains, confirming the parameter shapes for joint options like parent, aim, dir, up, and role, and verifying local-space direction keys (left, right, up, down, forward, back) used for head and jaw aiming. I'm also considering how to type a small helper function for getting chain tips, deciding whether to import Chain/Joint types or just rely on inline type inference to keep things simple.

Now I'm building out the skeleton structure—defining color/texture treatments for scales and egg speckling, then constructing the hip, spine, neck, and head joints and chains using catmull-rom paths with specific coordinates and parent-child relationships.

Continuing to the jaw and tail chains, then writing the leg loop that mirrors left and right sides, using polyline paths parented to the hips and checking tip/joint typing along the way.

Writing arm and wing loops...
